items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the New Science of Culture
items.authors: Douglas R. Guilbeault, Bhargav Srinivasa Desikan, James A. Evans
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.06240v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cognition and culture have long been treated as parallel objects of study, joined more by metaphor than by mechanism. We argue they are co-constituted in a manner now empirically tractable: subjectivities can be measured as local trajectories through a high-dimensional cultural field, and the field is itself the aggregate of those trajectories. Recent advances in machine learning, including embedding methods and large generative models, provide the first general framework for measuring this co-constitution from micro-cognition to macro-social structure. Vector geometry recovers individual conceptual structure, organizational communication, and large-scale ideologies; captures multimodal cultural content beyond text; and generates testable predictions about cultural emergence, including the simultaneous arrival of independent discoveries across distant minds. We treat this predictability of simultaneous innovation as evidence for the co- constitutive view: when the geometry of the cultural field is measurable, trajectories of cognitive search through it become predictable. We then examine generative AI agents as simulators of human subjectivity and as a qualitatively new coordinating substrate whose insertion into social life introduces evolutionary dynamics unprecedented in human cultural history. We formalize this reflexive condition as a Heisenberg-like Uncertainty Principle for generative AI: as instruments for fixing a culture's position grow more precise, our capacity to predict its trajectory degrades, because the machinery of cultural description and cultural action have merged. We close with ethical questions raised by AI-mediated cultural drift, recursive synthetic culture, and the limits of human cultural agency, offering guidelines for safe, equitable, and privacy-preserving research on AI and culture.
items.claude_summary: What happens to culture when the tools we use to describe it also generate it? This theoretical paper argues that cognition and culture are not separate phenomena but mutually constitutive: individual thought shapes collective meaning, and collective meaning shapes individual thought. Machine learning methods—embedding models and large generative AI—now make this loop empirically measurable for the first time. The authors use vector geometry to trace conceptual structures across individuals, organizations, and societies, and show that cultural dynamics can predict simultaneous independent discoveries across distant researchers. They then formalize a core risk: as generative AI becomes both the instrument for measuring culture and an active participant in producing it, a 'Heisenberg-like' uncertainty principle emerges—the more precisely AI fixes a culture's current state, the less predictable its trajectory becomes. The paper closes with ethical guidelines on AI-mediated cultural drift and human cultural agency.
items.centre_angle: This paper argues that generative AI has crossed a qualitative threshold: it is no longer merely a tool for analyzing culture but an agent that co-produces it, introducing a reflexivity that makes cultural trajectories fundamentally harder to predict. From CAMO's perspective on algorithmic foundations and trustworthy AI-driven decisions, the implication is sobering—when the measurement instrument and the phenomenon under study are the same system, standard assumptions about stable data-generating processes break down. Organizations and policymakers relying on AI-driven cultural or sentiment analytics should be alert to the possibility that the models informing their decisions are simultaneously reshaping the behavior those models purport to measure.

matched_camo.title: Seesaw Experimentation: A/B Tests with Spillovers
matched_camo.reason: Both papers grapple with measurement interventions that alter the system being measured—seesaw experimentation shows how optimizing a measured dimension degrades unmeasured ones, which is structurally analogous to the paper's Heisenberg-like principle that fixing a culture's position degrades trajectory prediction.

items.key_takeaway: Generative AI does not just measure culture—it actively reshapes it, making cultural trajectories less predictable the more precisely AI tries to fix them.
items.visual_concept: A single antique surveyor's theodolite positioned slightly off-center to the left on a plain stone surface, rendered in warm amber light from a low angle source to the right that casts a long clean shadow leftward across the frame. The instrument is the clear focal subject—precise, mechanical, built for fixing positions. Behind it, occupying the right half of the background, a gently blurred wide open landscape recedes toward a soft horizon, the terrain subtly shifting in hue from warm ochre near the instrument to a cooler, indeterminate blue-grey at the vanishing point, suggesting a future that grows less legible the further it extends. The contrast between the crisp clarity of the instrument in the foreground and the dissolving landscape behind it carries the paper's core tension: the act of precise measurement and the loss of predictive certainty. Palette is muted earth tones with a cool gradient horizon; lighting is soft directional daylight, no harsh shadows except the single elongated one from the theodolite.
red_flags: Preprint only—posted to arXiv, not yet peer-reviewed; theoretical claims have not undergone formal peer scrutiny.
The abstract is heavily conceptual and metaphor-driven (Heisenberg analogy, 'cultural field'); empirical validation of the core uncertainty principle claim is not evident from the excerpt alone.
Broad scope spanning philosophy of mind, cultural sociology, and AI may mean conclusions are too general to be actionable for a business or policy audience without significant translation.

items.title: Chaining Tasks, Redefining Work: A Theory of AI Automation
items.authors: Mert Demirer, John J. Horton, Nicole Immorlica, Brendan Lucier, Peyman Shahidi
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.15960v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We study the automation and productivity effects of AI when production is a sequence of interdependent steps with a Leontief structure. Each step can be executed manually by labor, augmented with AI, or automated within contiguous AI-executed steps called "chains." By characterizing the firm's cost-minimizing assignment of steps to humans and AI, we show that chaining can overturn comparative advantage logic, since human-advantaged steps may be optimally assigned to AI as part of a chain. Chaining also makes gains from automation depend on how AI-exposed steps cluster in the workflow beyond just how many there are, and can make the returns to improving AI quality non-monotone in a pattern resembling the productivity J-curve. Empirically, we show that existing automation patterns are consistent with the model's predictions: a step is more likely to be AI-executed when its neighbors are, and AI execution is more common where AI-exposed steps cluster in the workflow.
items.claude_summary: When AI automates work, the structure of the workflow matters as much as which individual steps AI can do well. This paper shows that AI tends to execute contiguous 'chains' of steps rather than isolated tasks — and this chaining logic can override simple comparative advantage: a step where humans outperform AI may still be handed to AI because it sits inside a chain of AI-executed steps. The implication is that automation exposure is not just a property of individual tasks but of their neighbours in a sequence. Empirically, steps adjacent to AI-executed steps are themselves more likely to be AI-executed, and gains from improving AI quality can be non-monotone, resembling a productivity J-curve where things get worse before they get better.
items.centre_angle: This paper argues that AI automation spreads through workflows via contiguous chaining, not task-by-task substitution — meaning the productivity impact of AI depends heavily on how AI-exposed steps are spatially arranged inside a production process, not merely how many there are. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, the implication is that firms designing AI rollouts around individual task exposure scores are likely to misread both the speed and distribution of automation gains. CAMO's case evidence from Decathlon China, where AI optimised individual coding tasks but left coordination bottlenecks untouched, illustrates the same structural point from the practitioner side: the gains live in the system architecture, not the task list.

matched_camo.title: Compressing Coordination with AI at Decathlon China
matched_camo.reason: Both the paper and the Decathlon case converge on the finding that AI's productivity impact is determined by workflow structure and inter-task dependencies rather than the automation of isolated steps.

matched_camo.title: Toward a Bad Job Economy: AI Adoption, Agency Costs, and Job Design
matched_camo.reason: The chaining model's implication that human-advantaged steps can be reassigned to AI connects directly to CAMO's analysis of how AI reshapes job boundaries and which tasks remain with workers under cost-minimising firm behaviour.

items.key_takeaway: Where AI-executable steps cluster in a workflow determines automation outcomes far more than a simple count of how many tasks AI can perform.
items.visual_concept: A single long assembly line rendered in cool industrial blues and greys, viewed from a slight elevation at one end so that it recedes toward a vanishing point at the far end of the frame — the line itself acts as the leading device drawing the eye deep into the image. In the foreground, roughly one-third of the line's stations glow with a steady warm amber light (the AI-executed chain), while the remaining stations are lit by cooler, dimmer overhead fluorescents. One human figure stands off-centre at the precise boundary between the lit and unlit sections, small relative to the machinery, looking down the chain. The surrounding space is a spare, uncluttered factory floor with no competing visual elements. Lighting is soft-industrial: diffuse overhead sources with the amber pool providing the only warmth in an otherwise cool, measured palette.
red_flags: Working paper on arXiv — not yet peer-reviewed; findings should be treated as preliminary.
Empirical validation relies on existing automation pattern data whose provenance is not described in the excerpt; readers cannot assess measurement quality from the abstract alone.

items.title: How AI Is Changing Innovation: Why Speed Alone Isn’t a Strategy
items.summary: AI is making it faster and cheaper than ever to turn ideas into prototypes, products, and businesses—but that abundance creates new challenges for leaders. In episode 3 of a special four-part series on how AI is changing leadership, we look at the ways industry leaders are using AI to truly gain a competitive edge and innovate for the future. Cisco Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel explains how AI is changing the pace and nature of innovation, why human judgment and taste become more important when everyone has access to the same tools, and how companies can use AI to tackle problems they couldn't have solved before. He also discusses the risks of AI agents, why organizations need new approaches to security and oversight, and how leaders can build a culture that embraces experimentation without sacrificing rigor or accountability.
items.claude_summary: When AI makes prototyping faster and cheaper for everyone, speed stops being a differentiator. This HBR IdeaCast episode features Cisco's Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel arguing that the real competitive edge shifts to human judgment and 'taste'—the ability to decide which ideas are worth pursuing—rather than the ability to execute them quickly. Patel also raises the governance side: AI agents introduce new security and oversight requirements that organizations are not yet equipped to handle. The episode frames innovation leadership less as a technical challenge and more as a cultural and strategic one, where experimentation culture and accountability structures matter as much as the tools themselves. Note: this is a podcast episode, so claims are practitioner assertions rather than empirically tested findings.
items.centre_angle: This podcast episode argues that when AI commoditizes the execution of ideas, the scarce resource becomes strategic judgment—knowing which problems to solve and which directions to pursue. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, this reframing has real organizational consequences: firms that treat AI as a speed tool without redesigning decision rights and accountability structures risk a flood of low-value output rather than genuine innovation. CAMO's work on the Decathlon China case offers a complementary data point—accelerating task execution without compressing coordination bottlenecks produced only marginal system-level gains, suggesting that the limiting factor in AI-enabled innovation is rarely the technology itself.

matched_camo.title: Compressing Coordination with AI at Decathlon China
matched_camo.reason: Both the episode and the Decathlon case make the same structural point: AI optimizes task execution but the system-level payoff depends on what happens between tasks—coordination, judgment, and strategic prioritization.

items.key_takeaway: When AI gives everyone the same execution capability, competitive advantage moves upstream to the quality of human judgment about which problems are worth solving.
items.visual_concept: A single wooden compass—the drafting instrument—centered slightly left of frame in close-up foreground, resting on a large blank white drafting table that recedes to a vanishing point at the right edge of the image. The compass is the clear focal subject; the empty table surface beyond it is uncluttered and slightly out of focus, emphasizing openness and the problem of choosing direction rather than executing it. A single overhead drafting lamp pools cool white light directly onto the compass, with the surrounding table falling into soft shadow. The palette is spare: warm brass of the compass against the cool grey-white of the table surface, suggesting precision tools in an environment of open, unresolved possibility.
red_flags: Podcast episode, not peer-reviewed or empirically grounded—all claims are practitioner opinion from a single executive (Cisco CPO).
Potential conflict of interest: Jeetu Patel speaks for a major technology vendor with commercial interests in AI adoption narratives.
RSS excerpt is thin; substantive claims may not be fully represented here, and the full episode is behind HBR's access wall.

items.title: Large Language Models and Augmented Democracy
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.04412v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Artificial intelligence enables computational agents to represent political preferences and take part in collective decision-making. In this thesis, I investigate the opportunities and challenges of digital twins (DTs) based on Large Language Models (LLMs) as intermediaries in augmented democracy, focusing on individual preference representation, collective representation of political organizations, and the vulnerability of those representations to attackers. First, using data from an online experiment in Brazil, I examine whether personalized DTs can predict citizens' preferences for unseen policy proposals. Second, I extend the DT framework from individuals to political organizations. Using Swiss parliamentary data, I build topic-specific knowledge graphs from lawmakers' legislative records and connect them to LLM-based lawmaker agents, which are organized into party-level DTs representing collective positions. Agentic deliberation among these agents tests whether aggregated party representations capture a broader range of intra-party perspectives than official party communications. Finally, I study the vulnerability and robustness of LLM-mediated deliberation against prompt-injection attacks that amplify viewpoints, suppress opinions, or redirect consensus. Using data from a 2023 deliberative experiment in the United Kingdom, I analyze how attack effectiveness varies with the distribution of opinions and rhetorical strategies, and evaluate a pipeline combining injection detection, structured opinion representations, and reinforcement learning to improve resistance. These findings characterize the opportunities and challenges of LLM-based digital twins in augmented democracy, stressing accurate preference representation, faithful aggregation, and robustness to strategic interaction.
items.claude_summary: Can AI-powered digital twins reliably represent citizens' political preferences in collective decision-making? This thesis investigates three dimensions of LLM-based 'augmented democracy': whether personalized digital twins predict individual policy preferences (tested with Brazilian survey data), whether aggregated party-level agents capture intra-party diversity better than official communications (tested with Swiss parliamentary records), and how vulnerable LLM-mediated deliberation is to prompt-injection attacks that distort or suppress viewpoints (tested with UK deliberative experiment data). Across all three, the work finds genuine promise alongside serious risks — particularly that adversarial manipulation of LLM deliberation is feasible and that its effectiveness varies with opinion distribution and rhetorical strategy. A detection-plus-reinforcement-learning pipeline is proposed to improve robustness.
items.centre_angle: This thesis asks whether LLMs can act as faithful intermediaries for human preferences in political deliberation — a representational accuracy problem that sits squarely within CAMO's interest in the statistical and algorithmic foundations of trustworthy AI-driven decisions. The findings on prompt-injection vulnerability are particularly instructive: even well-designed aggregation pipelines can be gamed by adversarial inputs, echoing the self-fulfilling and reinforcement biases that CAMO's own algorithmic work has documented in commercial decision systems. The democratic deliberation setting is novel, but the underlying question — under what conditions can an AI system faithfully aggregate heterogeneous human inputs without systematic distortion — is one any organisation deploying AI for preference elicitation or collective sensemaking should take seriously.

matched_camo.title: Dynamic Selection in Algorithmic Decision-making
matched_camo.reason: Both papers are concerned with how endogenous or adversarial inputs to an algorithmic system can systematically bias its outputs — self-fulfilling bias in bandit algorithms maps conceptually onto prompt-injection bias in LLM deliberation pipelines.

items.key_takeaway: LLMs can approximate collective political preferences, but their deliberative outputs are vulnerable to adversarial manipulation in ways that demand detection and correction mechanisms before any real-world deployment.
items.visual_concept: A single large ballot box or classical urn rendered in pale stone, positioned slightly left of center in the frame and occupying the middle ground. Behind it, a single strong vanishing point draws a grid of receding lines — suggesting a chamber floor or tiled civic hall — that converge directly behind the urn, anchoring it as the compositional focus. The surrounding space is sparse and architectural: high bare walls, no figures, no clutter. Lighting is cool and directional, a shaft of daylight entering from the upper right, casting a sharp shadow from the urn leftward across the floor. The palette is muted civic grey and warm ivory, with a faint luminous tint on the urn's surface suggesting something active or contested within it.
red_flags: Unpublished thesis posted to arXiv — not peer-reviewed and findings have not undergone formal external scrutiny.
Empirical bases span three different national contexts (Brazil, Switzerland, UK) with distinct political systems; generalisability across settings is uncertain.
Abstract does not report effect sizes or confidence intervals for the preference-prediction accuracy claims, making it difficult to assess practical significance.
The reinforcement-learning robustness pipeline is described as a proposal; it is unclear whether it has been validated against real adversarial actors.

items.title: How AI Is Changing Talent, Not Just Tasks: Rethinking Where Human Judgment Matters Most
items.summary: The decisions leaders must make about AI today go far beyond what platforms to invest in: AI is changing organizational culture and leadership for good. In episode 1 of a special four-part series on how AI is changing leadership, we look at how the technology is changing how people interact at work, the new culture it is creating, and how leaders can get smart about talent management and strategy in this rapidly advancing world. Paula Goldman, Salesforce’s chief ethical and humane use officer, argues there's currently a big opportunity to redesign work around the complementary strengths of humans and AI. She explains how AI could reshape entry-level jobs and the development of future leaders, why companies need to rethink internal mobility and talent development, and how executives can prepare their organizations for an AI-powered workforce without sacrificing accountability, creativity, or trust. Goldman is the author of Manage the Machine: How to Harness Human-AI Collaboration at Work.
items.claude_summary: As AI takes over more routine and structured work, the question of where human judgment remains essential is moving to the center of organizational strategy. This HBR IdeaCast episode features Paula Goldman, Salesforce's chief ethical and humane use officer, arguing that the current moment offers a genuine opportunity to redesign work around human-AI complementarity rather than simply substituting AI for labor. Goldman focuses on three concrete concerns: how entry-level roles are being reshaped in ways that may undercut traditional leadership development pipelines, why internal mobility and talent development frameworks need rethinking, and how executives can maintain accountability, creativity, and trust as AI becomes embedded in daily operations. The discussion is practitioner-oriented and draws on Goldman's book. No empirical findings are cited in the excerpt.
items.centre_angle: This podcast argues that AI is not merely automating discrete tasks but restructuring the developmental pathways through which people become capable leaders—particularly at the entry level. From CAMO's perspective on AI & Jobs, this concern is well-founded: our research on the hidden social penalties of AI use at work shows that adoption decisions are shaped by organizational culture and interpersonal evaluation, not just technical capability, suggesting that talent development frameworks need to account for these dynamics explicitly. The question of how firms maintain accountability and grow future leaders in an AI-augmented environment is also central to CAMO's work on job design, where AI adoption can erode the high-effort, high-skill roles that traditionally serve as training grounds.

matched_camo.reason: Both pieces examine how organizational culture and social evaluation shape whether and how employees engage with AI tools, with particular relevance to career development and accountability.
matched_camo.title: Research: The Hidden Penalty of Using AI at Work

matched_camo.reason: The podcast's concern that AI may hollow out entry-level developmental roles connects directly to this paper's finding that AI can displace high-effort, high-skill positions even when those roles generate more total surplus.
matched_camo.title: Toward a Bad Job Economy: AI Adoption, Agency Costs, and Job Design

items.key_takeaway: AI is restructuring the entry-level roles that have historically produced senior leaders, and companies that treat this as purely a technology question will find themselves short of capable judgment at the top.
items.visual_concept: A single wooden ladder, centered in the frame and photographed straight-on, standing upright against a plain pale concrete wall in an otherwise empty room. The lower rungs are missing or have been replaced by flat, featureless aluminum bars — visually smooth and indistinct — while the upper rungs remain hand-worn wood. The background is uncluttered — bare floor, bare wall — so the ladder reads cleanly as the sole subject. The mood is calm but slightly uneasy: the path upward is intact, but the entry point has changed in character.

Paula Goldman is a Salesforce executive and author with a book to promote; potential conflict of interest should be noted.
Not peer-reviewed; practitioner opinion piece in podcast format.

items.title: How AI Is Changing Communication: Weighing Efficiency with Efficacy
items.summary: AI is rapidly changing how top leaders communicate with employees, customers, boards, and each other. In episode 2 of a special four-part series on how AI is changing leadership, we explore how executives can use AI to improve communication without outsourcing the thinking, judgment, and empathy that make it effective. Stanford professor Matt Abrahams and Zapier CEO Wade Foster discuss how leaders are using AI to synthesize information, structure ideas, prepare for difficult conversations, and rehearse for high-stakes moments. They also explain why leaders should be wary of letting AI write everything for them, how overreliance on AI can create a “comprehension gap,” and why preserving a distinctive human voice may become even more important as AI-generated communication becomes ubiquitous. Abrahams is the author of Think Faster, Talk Smarter and host of the podcast Think Fast, Talk Smart. Foster is the cofounder and CEO of Zapier, a software automation company.
items.claude_summary: As AI tools become standard aids for drafting, summarizing, and rehearsing communication, a central question emerges: what happens to leadership quality when executives outsource too much of the cognitive work behind their words? Stanford professor Matt Abrahams and Zapier CEO Wade Foster argue that AI can legitimately help leaders structure ideas and prepare for high-stakes conversations, but warn that over-reliance creates a 'comprehension gap' — leaders who can deliver AI-polished messages they don't fully own. The conversation centers on preserving authentic voice and independent judgment even as AI-generated text becomes ubiquitous. The discussion is practitioner-focused and draws on personal experience rather than systematic research.
items.centre_angle: This podcast episode raises a behavioral question that sits at the heart of AI adoption inside organizations: when AI handles the production of communication, does the underlying thinking atrophy? From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, the concern mirrors a broader pattern we observe across deployment contexts — efficiency gains at the task level can quietly erode the organizational capabilities those tasks were meant to exercise. CAMO's work on the 'comprehension gap' dynamic in professional settings, including findings from the hidden-penalty research on how AI use is socially perceived, suggests that the reputational and cognitive stakes of AI-assisted communication are real and deserve more rigorous study than practitioner reflection alone can provide.

matched_camo.reason: Both pieces grapple with how AI-assisted output is perceived by others and what signals AI use sends about the person behind it — the podcast's 'authentic voice' concern is a first-person version of the competence-penalty dynamic documented in the CAMO experiment.
matched_camo.title: Research: The Hidden Penalty of Using AI at Work

items.key_takeaway: AI can scaffold how leaders communicate, but executives who let it replace rather than support their reasoning risk delivering polished messages they do not genuinely understand or own.
items.visual_concept: A single wooden lectern, centered in a spare auditorium, shot from a low angle so it dominates the foreground against a receding row of empty seats that form parallel leading lines drawing the eye toward it. The palette is muted grey-blue with warm amber pooling on the lectern face, suggesting the tension between institutional setting and individual voice.

No named authors in the RSS metadata; attribution relies on guest identification from episode description.

items.title: AI is changing work. Now it has to change the organization
items.summary: The first phase of enterprise AI put powerful new tools in people’s hands. Capturing the larger opportunity from agentic AI will require leaders to rethink the shape of the organization itself.
items.claude_summary: Enterprise AI has moved through an initial phase of equipping individuals with better tools. The larger gains, McKinsey argues, now require redesigning the organization itself — its structures, roles, and decision-making architecture — to accommodate agentic AI systems that act, coordinate, and execute across functions. The article contends that firms still operating AI as a layer on top of existing org designs will capture only a fraction of the available value. The shift being described is from AI-as-tool to AI-as-organizational-actor, with implications for how work is divided, how accountability is assigned, and how managers oversee processes they no longer fully execute. The excerpt is brief, so specific empirical claims cannot be verified from available text.
items.centre_angle: This McKinsey article argues that the structural redesign of organizations — not further investment in individual AI tools — is the next critical frontier for enterprise AI value. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, this resonates with a pattern evident across our case research: organizations that automate tasks without rethinking coordination architecture see bounded gains. Our Decathlon China case illustrates exactly this — coding efficiency rose 20–40%, yet overall delivery speed improved only 10–15% because the bottleneck was coordination between tasks, not execution of them. The implication for leaders is that agentic AI raises the stakes on organizational design decisions that most firms have yet to seriously address.

matched_camo.title: Compressing Coordination with AI at Decathlon China
matched_camo.reason: Directly illustrates the article's core claim: task-level AI efficiency does not translate to organizational-level gains without structural redesign of coordination.

items.key_takeaway: Capturing the full value of agentic AI requires redesigning organizational structures and accountability, not just deploying better tools on top of existing ones.

items.title: How to Outcompete Your Client’s AI
items.authors:
José Parra-Moyano, Karl Schmedders, Olivier Laplace, and Benjamin Torben-Nielsen.

José Parra-Moyano is a professor of digital strategy at the International Institute for Management Development (IMD) in Lausanne, Switzerland. Karl Schmedders is a professor of finance at IMD in Lausanne. Olivier Laplace is a partner at Vi Partners. Benjamin Torben-Nielsen is a strategy and portfolio leader at Roche.
items.summary: Andy Carter/Ikon Images The in-house lawyers at real estate investment firm Alturas Capital Partners used to rely on outside counsel for much of its lease work. Thanks to generative AI, it can now do that work internally, saving the firm hundreds of thousands of dollars in spending and compressing lease work that once stalled for […]
items.claude_summary: When clients deploy generative AI to handle work they previously outsourced, professional service firms face direct displacement. This article examines how outside counsel at a real estate investment firm lost lease-review work to the client's in-house AI, and asks what service providers must do to remain competitive. The core argument is that professionals need to identify where AI-assisted clients still have blind spots — complexity, judgment calls, cross-jurisdictional risk — and reposition their value accordingly. The article is based on practitioner observation rather than systematic research, and the RSS excerpt is thin, so specific prescriptions cannot be confirmed without full access.
items.centre_angle: This article surfaces a structural shift in professional services: AI is not just changing what workers do inside firms, it is relocating tasks across firm boundaries — pulling work from outside counsel back in-house and reshaping the market for expert labor. From CAMO's perspective on AI & Jobs, this mirrors the displacement logic explored in our research on the hidden social penalties of AI use: the question is not only whether professionals can do the work, but whether clients will continue to pay for it once AI lowers the cost of doing it themselves. The careers most at risk are those whose value proposition rests on routine expert execution rather than judgment under genuine uncertainty.

matched_camo.reason: Both pieces examine how AI reshapes the perceived and actual value of professional expertise — one inside the firm, the other across firm boundaries — raising parallel questions about where expert credibility survives AI diffusion.

matched_camo.title: Toward a Bad Job Economy: AI Adoption, Agency Costs, and Job Design
matched_camo.reason: The article's premise — that AI erodes the commercial rationale for high-skill outsourced work — parallels CAMO's finding that AI disproportionately lowers the cost of satisfactory performance, compressing returns on expertise and potentially degrading job quality across the market.

items.key_takeaway: When clients gain AI capable of handling routine expert work in-house, professional service providers must reanchor their value on judgment under complexity — or lose the mandate entirely.

items.title: Representational Control over Self-Report & Behavior Coherence in LLM Risk-Taking
items.authors: Rafal Kocielnik, Peiyang Song, Pengrui Han, Myrl G. Marmarelis, Ramit Debnath, Dean Mobbs, R. Michael Alvarez
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.04125v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Self-report is an appealing low-cost probe of an LLM's dispositions, but recent work finds only selective agreement between what models report and how they behave. Prior accounts establish these patterns by prompting black-box LLMs, leaving open whether the gap is a prompting artefact or a fact about how the underlying constructs are represented internally. We investigate risk-taking, a consequential dimension of agentic decision-making, using activation steering to measure self-report and behavior under the same internal intervention. We survey nine steering-vector extraction methods spanning task-specific directives, the model's own task behavior, and dispositional descriptions at two granularities, evaluated on two behavioral tasks and two psychometric instruments across four open-weight LLMs. We find that (1) a shared internal intervention does not ensure shared responsiveness: directions built from trait descriptions move self-report but leave behavior at chance, directions built from the model's own task choices do the reverse, and only task-specific directives reach both, weakly. (2) Diagnosis dissolves that exception: removing surface confounders leaves the directives only 32% of their behavioral effect. The two channels are otherwise steered by near-orthogonal directions, each channel reachable by several independent constructions. (3) An intervention composing one behavior-moving and one self-report-moving direction moves both together; flipping one sign sets them in opposition, with reported and enacted risk pointing in opposite directions on 69-89% of flipped compositions in all models. These findings move the self-report-behavior relationship from a black-box observation to a representational one that can be inspected and controlled, motivating representational checks alongside behavioral evaluation.
items.claude_summary: When a large language model says it would take a risk, does that prediction match what it actually does? This study moves beyond black-box prompting to examine the internal representations driving self-reported and behaviorally enacted risk-taking in LLMs. Using activation steering across nine vector-extraction methods and four open-weight models, researchers find that self-report and behavior are governed by near-orthogonal internal directions — meaning the two channels are largely independent. Task-specific directives weakly reach both, but removing surface confounders strips away most of that behavioral effect. Critically, composing one behavior-moving and one self-report-moving direction can deliberately set the two in opposition, producing models that report low risk while acting high-risk (or vice versa) in 69–89% of cases. The finding reframes the self-report–behavior gap as a structural, inspectable representational property rather than a prompting artifact.
items.centre_angle: This study demonstrates that LLM self-report and behavioral output are steered by near-orthogonal internal representations, meaning a model's stated dispositions are an unreliable proxy for its actual decision-making behavior. From CAMO's perspective on algorithmic foundations for trustworthy AI-driven decisions, this has direct implications for any organization using LLM self-assessment as a shortcut for auditing agentic AI behavior — a practice that is both common and, on this evidence, structurally flawed. The finding motivates representational audits alongside behavioral evaluation, raising the bar for what counts as adequate AI governance in enterprise deployments.

matched_camo.reason: Both papers probe the gap between what an AI system appears to communicate and what is actually driving its outputs — one through interpretability and attribution in medical AI, the other through internal representational structure in LLMs — with shared implications for how much humans can trust AI self-presentation.

items.key_takeaway: An LLM's stated risk appetite and its actual risk-taking behavior are governed by separate internal mechanisms, so asking a model to describe itself is not a reliable substitute for observing what it does.

items.title: AI is changing how we work. Is your organization ready?
items.summary: As AI reshapes roles, leaders face a bigger question: how to rethink jobs, teams, and the way work gets done in a fundamentally different era.
items.claude_summary: As AI reshapes roles and workflows, organizations face a structural question that goes beyond tool adoption: how to redesign jobs, teams, and operating models for a fundamentally different era of work. The article, from McKinsey's People & Organization practice, argues that leaders must move from ad hoc AI experimentation to deliberate rethinking of how work is organized. The RSS excerpt is brief and the full article is not reproduced here, so specific findings cannot be confirmed. Based on available signals, the piece appears to address workforce readiness, role redefinition, and organizational design — themes that sit squarely at the intersection of AI adoption and job architecture.
items.centre_angle: This McKinsey piece raises a question CAMO's own survey evidence takes seriously: AI adoption at the tool level consistently outpaces readiness at the organizational level. The Deloitte-HKU AI Adoption Index 2026 found that the dominant barriers to realizing AI value are organizational and executional — siloed departments, cultural resistance, and poor data quality — not technical limitations. The implication is that leaders who treat AI as an infrastructure problem, rather than a job-design and coordination problem, are likely to keep reporting the ROI gap that nearly half of C-suite executives in that survey acknowledged.
